DRAFTScrewworm zone freedom model

Screwworm zone freedom model (draft)

What the tool estimates: the model estimate of the chance (draft) that a control zone is free of New World screwworm over time after its last detection, given that surveillance finds nothing more. It is a proof-of-concept model.

Do not cite these numbers as evidence of absence or freedom, for release, trade or reporting. They are outputs of a draft model under assumed rates. APHIS declares freedom by time since the last detection, with fly trapping and animal inspection; this model has no fly trapping (what the model leaves out).

What "free" means: absolute absence, that is, no infected unit in the population. This is distinct from effective absence, where prevalence is below a chosen design prevalence. The model follows the zero-inflated freedom model (Preventive Veterinary Medicine, 2026, 106892). For screwworm the unit is a farm: the zone is free when none of its farms is infested. Where a card says "freedom", it means this model estimate, not freedom as APHIS declares it (the APHIS criterion).

Free of infested premises, not of flies: "free" here means no infested premises in the zone. It does not mean there are no flies in the environment.

The model in brief

The model has five components: introductions, season, one farm, the zone, and how infested farms are found. The model at a glance, the next card, shows them with one picture each. The worked example is one county, Zavala County, Texas.

Chance the zone is free at the last inspection round (day 360, May), model estimate (draft): 85 percent. Over the run it moves between 85 percent (July) and 94 percent (January). The rise in the cold months comes from fewer flies arriving, not from stronger evidence, and it falls back when the weather warms. Read the warm-season value. It does not stay at or above the 95 percent reference line (for illustration) to the end of the run.

Changed 2026-11-18: the model now has an introduction module and a season, and its worked example is one Texas county. Each parameter card opens with one line. Every change is listed in what changed in this version.

The interactive app shows the estimate for any setting of the inputs.

How the parameter values were reached, and what has been checked

AI models (Anthropic Claude) searched the literature, extracted the numbers, chose each value and range, and wrote the parameter and source cards. The model's developers set the scenario and directed the work. No value has been checked by a screwworm subject-matter expert.

  • Quotes: every quote was matched by machine against the retrieved text of its source. Of the 82 quotes on the 61 source cards, 70 found word for word, 5 near matches, 5 not found (not shown), 2 with no full text to check. A found quote shows that the source says it, not that the value is right. The 61 source cards are 38 distinct documents: the same document cited for different numbers has one card per use, and each source card names the other cards for its document.
  • Sources: every source on five of the most influential parameter cards was read against its card by an AI model: 31 uses, 21 support, 7 partly, 1 does not support, 2 could not be opened (the source census).
  • Arithmetic: two independent implementations of the model agree within simulation error (the agreement check).

The model at a glance

The model has five components. Read them in this order.

  1. 1Introductions

    New infested farms come from three sources: flies arriving, moved animals and wildlife. Season, sterile-fly coverage, nearby detections and mitigations scale them month by month.

    Open the card

  2. 2Season

    Fly activity follows the monthly temperature of the county. A cold month brings fewer introductions, which is lower pressure and not stronger evidence.

    Open the card

  3. 3One farm

    On an infested farm the infestation passes from animal to animal until it runs its course. The animals carrying larvae are the ones that inspections and owners can find.

    Open the card

  4. 4The zone

    The zone is a set of farms, here the 114 farms of one Texas county. Infested farms are added by introductions and by spread between farms.

    Open the card

  5. 5How infested farms are found

    Inspection rounds examine a sample of animals on a sample of farms, and owners report wounds they see at a close look. A positive fly trap counts as a detection, and empty traps give no credit.

    Open the card

How they connect: the introduction module and the season set how often a new infested farm appears. The farm and zone components carry the infestation forward. Detection is what the clean results are judged against: each clean inspection round, and each day without an owner report, raises the chance that no farm is infested.

The worked example is Zavala County, Texas. Every parameter is in the parameter table.

How infested farms are found

How to read the detection picture

  • "Channel 1: inspection rounds": "A round visits a sample of farms", "The inspector examines a sample of animals" and "An infested animal is found".
  • "Channel 2: owner reporting": a chain of four steps, "A wound becomes visible", "The owner's next close look", "The owner reports" and "The laboratory confirms". The second step is new in this version.
  • "Confirmed detection": both channels end here, and it "Ends the freedom estimate".
  • "Outside the model: fly traps": the dashed box. "A positive trap = a detection" and "Empty traps = no credit toward freedom".

Two surveillance streams look for infested farms: owners who report a wound, and inspection rounds. Both find only animals in the "Infested" (larvae hatched) step of the farm picture: "Inspection misses eggs", so an animal in the "Latent" (eggs laid) step cannot be found by either stream. Labels in quotes are those printed on the detection, farm and zone pictures.

Stream 1, owner reports

Drawn as "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture and "Owner reports" on the zone picture. Owners can report at any time, including between inspection rounds.

  • A wound becomes visible: the share of infested animals with a visible wound ramps up over the first days after the farm is infested (mean clinical onset time), to a ceiling (share of wounds visible).
  • The owner looks closely: on a large ranch the owner does not see every animal closely every day. A visible wound waits for the owner's next close look, on average half the days between the owner's close looks: 3.5 days at the scenario value of 7 days.
  • The owner notices it: each visible wound is noticed with a set chance (chance the owner notices a wound).
  • The detection is confirmed: once a wound is noticed, the confirmed detection follows after a random delay that averages the owner reporting delay.

So owner reporting strengthens as more animals carry visible wounds, but is capped by how quickly a noticed wound becomes a confirmed detection.

How much rests on owner reports

On the county scenario the model estimate of the chance the zone is free at the last round (day 360, draft) is 85 percent. It is 40 percent if owners never report, which leaves the inspection rounds alone. The app shows the second number beside the first.

On the earlier six-month scenario, which has 100 farms and constant rates, the estimate at day 180 is 89 percent with close looks every 7 days and 36 percent if owners never report. With close looks every day, as the model assumed before this version, it was 93 percent. All these numbers were computed with the analytic (closed-form) build of this version.

What the app shows about detection

Under a "Planning" heading, apart from the freedom result, the app shows the box "Chance of no detection by day 360 (before any results)". It is about 2 percent on the county scenario, and about 10 percent by day 180 on the six-month scenario. It is a projection made at the start, before any inspection result, and it is not part of the freedom estimate. Three different numbers are easy to confuse. Each is named here once, with its value at day 180 on the six-month scenario:

  • The chance of no detection by the last round: the Planning box, about 10 percent.
  • The chance the zone is free and nothing was detected: the dashed line on the app's graph, about 9 percent.
  • The chance the zone is free with no surveillance at all: about 25 percent. Neither stream operates, so nothing can be detected.

The freedom result itself is a fourth number: the chance the zone is free given that nothing was detected.

Stream 2, inspection rounds

Drawn as "Inspection: a sample of animals" on the farm picture and "Inspection rounds" on the zone picture. On set dates a round visits a set number of farms, drawn at random, and on each visited farm examines a set number of animals (the whole herd if it is smaller). Each infested animal examined is found with a set chance (inspection sensitivity), and a visited farm is found if any of its examined animals is. An infested farm a round visits but does not find is drawn as "Missed" on the zone picture. The round dates, the farms per round and the animals per farm are fixed in the county scenario.

Fly traps

Drawn as "Outside the model: fly traps" on the detection picture. The rule is: a positive fly trap counts as a confirmed detection, and the freedom estimate no longer applies once a trap is positive. Empty traps give no credit toward freedom, because traps can catch nothing in an area that has cases. A trap channel is not built in this version.

What counts as a detection

A detection in the model is a confirmed detection. A suspect larva or report is taken to be followed by laboratory identification, which tells screwworm larvae from those of other flies that look alike in the field, so the model has no false alarms. The model has no separate laboratory step. A round that finds nothing, and each day with no owner report, count as evidence: the chance that no farm is infested is updated after each.

After the first confirmed detection

  • The found farm: drawn as "Found" on the zone picture and as "Farm found" on the farm picture; finding it starts lockdown.
  • The estimate: "Chance no farm is infested" on the zone picture is conditional on no detection so far; a confirmed detection ends it.
  • Lockdown: "Initiate lockdown" switches spread between farms to the dot-dash "Spread reduced after lockdown" arrow: spread between farms is multiplied by the lockdown spread multiplier for the rest of the time the model runs. It stands for more sterile flies and tighter movement controls. The model does not lift it.
  • Release: from the detection on, every counted farm is released at a steady rate, on average 21 days after the detection, or after its own infestation if that comes later (zone clearance time). Neither picture draws this.

Parameters for detection

  • Owner reporting delay: "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture and "Owner reports" on the zone picture, as the delay from noticing to a confirmed detection
  • Chance the owner notices a wound: "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture and "Owner reports" on the zone picture, as the chance an owner notices a visible wound
  • Days between the owner's close looks at the animals: "The owner's next close look" on the detection picture
  • Share of wounds visible: not drawn; it acts through "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture (the share of wounds on infested animals that ever become visible)
  • Mean clinical onset time: not drawn; it acts through "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture (how fast wounds on infested animals become visible)
  • Inspection sensitivity: "Inspection: a sample of animals" on the farm picture and "Inspection rounds" on the zone picture, as the chance an inspector finds an infested animal; an infested farm a round does not find is drawn as "Missed"

One farm: spread inside a farm

How to read the farm picture

  • "Animals on one infested farm": the animals move from Susceptible to Latent (eggs laid), Infested (larvae hatched) and Recovered. Every infested farm runs the same course.
  • The loop "their flies lay eggs on more animals": spread from infested animals to susceptible animals on the same farm. Its branch to "Other farms in the zone" is spread between farms, shown on the zone picture.
  • "Inspection misses eggs": an animal in the Latent step cannot be found.
  • "Finds the farm": "Inspection: a sample of animals" and "Owner reports a wound" both act on infested animals. Either leads to "Farm found", which starts lockdown in the zone.

The two ways the farm is found, "Finds the farm", are described in how infested farms are found. Spread to "Other farms in the zone" is on the zone card.

In this version: the season does not act inside a farm. Eggs and larvae are on the host at body temperature, so the course inside a farm is the same in every month. The slowing of fly generations on a farm in winter is left out. In the county scenario every farm has 100 animals, although the herds of the county differ widely in size.

Parameters for spread inside a farm

  • Within-premises doubling time: the Susceptible to Latent step on the farm picture, driven by the "their flies lay eggs on more animals" loop from Infested
  • Within-premises recovery time: the Infested to Recovered step on the farm picture; it also sets when the infestation on a farm has run its course
  • Mean latent time: the Latent to Infested step on the farm picture

The model has no fly population: the loop "their flies lay eggs on more animals" is spread from animal to animal on the farm. An infested farm leaves the count when its infestation runs its course, whether or not it is found. After a confirmed detection, every farm still counted is also released at a steady rate, on average 21 days after the detection. Neither picture draws these two exits.

The zone: introductions, spread between farms and release

How to read the zone picture

  • Left, "Adds infested farms": the three inputs that add infested farms to the zone: "Already infested at start", "New arrivals from outside" and "Spread between farms".
  • Left, "Finds them": the two surveillance streams, "Inspection rounds" and "Owner reports".
  • Middle, "Farms in the zone": an open circle is a farm that is not infested; an orange dot is an infested farm not yet found; a dashed blue ring is a farm visited by an inspection round. "Missed" is an infested farm the round did not find; "Found" is a confirmed detection.
  • Arrows in the farm grid: a solid orange arrow is spread between farms. The found farm sends a blue arrow to "Initiate lockdown", which switches spread to the dot-dash "Spread reduced after lockdown" arrow.
  • Right, "Chance no farm is infested": the model estimate, given that searching finds nothing more, so no lockdown, plotted against the time since the last detection.
  • Right, "Expected new infested farms" and "Expected cost": counted over all outcomes, so lockdown lowers them; projected from the start, with placeholder cost weights.
  • Bottom line, "Not modeled": processes the model does not represent.

"Finds them", "Missed", "Found" and "Initiate lockdown" are described in how infested farms are found. What happens inside one infested farm is on the farm card.

In this version: "New arrivals from outside" and "Spread between farms" no longer run at constant rates. Every 30 days of the run each is multiplied by a factor from the introduction module. Introductions follow the season, sterile-fly coverage, nearby detections and mitigations. Spread between farms follows fly activity, sterile-fly coverage, preventive treatment and, on the share carried by moved animals, movement checks. The lockdown cut after a detection still applies on top. In the county scenario the zone is the 114 farms of the county.

Parameters for introductions, spread between farms and release

  • Introduction interval: "New arrivals from outside" on the zone picture
  • Zone doubling time: "Spread between farms" on the zone picture, drawn as the solid orange arrow in the farm grid (legend: "Between-farm spread")
  • Lockdown spread multiplier: the dot-dash "Spread reduced after lockdown" arrow on the zone picture, which "Initiate lockdown" switches on once a farm is found
  • Zone clearance time: not drawn; after a confirmed detection (a farm drawn as "Found" on the zone picture), every farm still counted is released on this clock

An infested farm leaves the count when its infestation runs its course, whether or not it is found. After a confirmed detection, every farm still counted is also released at a steady rate, on average 21 days after the detection. The picture does not draw these two exits.

The county scenario: fixed inputs and results

This is the scenario the app opens on. A number on this page is for it where the card says "the county scenario". A card marked "computed before this version" uses the earlier six-month scenario, described at the end of this card. Why this county, and its census and detection data, are on the county.

Fixed inputs

Zone114 farms, the operations with cattle of Zavala County, Texas, each taken as one farm of 100 animals (the county).
FreedomAbsolute: zero infested farms, not a prevalence below a threshold.
Period360 days, which is 12 months in steps of 30 days, from the last detection in the county. The clock starts in June.
Surveillance12 inspection rounds, one every 30 days; 23 farms visited per round; 30 animals examined on each visited farm. Owner reporting runs all the time, with the owner looking closely at the animals every 7 days. Streams the model does not use are listed below.
Start (day 0, the last detection)The number of infested farms nobody has found is drawn with mean 1 (Poisson), so the zone starts free with chance 0.37; their infestations are about 14 days old (exponential, mean 14 days). Both are guesses: no source estimates the undetected remainder.
Controls in force at day 0Quarantine and movement controls are not states of the model. Spread between farms starts from its uncontrolled rate (zone doubling time 24 days, a figure for no control in the warm season) and is scaled each month by fly activity. Sterile-fly coverage, movement checks and preventive treatment are inputs, at the values in the second table. The lockdown cut switches on only at a new confirmed detection.
IntroductionsThe introduction module is on. The reference rate is one new infested farm about every 130 days. It was counted per county, for a free county next to an active quarantine zone in summer 2026, and the zone here is one county. The module scales it month by month. With nearby detections at 1.5, the rate in a warm month is 1.425 times the reference, about one new infested farm every 91 days. In January it is 0.574 times the reference (season).
ParametersThe twelve earlier parameters and the days between close looks at their central values (the parameter table). The inputs of the introduction module are in the second table.

Headline results

Chance the zone is free at the last inspection round (day 360, May), model estimate (draft): 85 percent. Over the run it moves between 85 percent (July) and 94 percent (January). The rise in the cold months comes from fewer flies arriving, not from stronger evidence, and it falls back when the weather warms. Read the warm-season value. It does not stay at or above the 95 percent reference line (for illustration) to the end of the run.

  • If owners never report: the estimate at the last round is 40 percent. That leaves the inspection rounds alone.
  • Chance of no detection by day 360, before any results: about 2 percent. It is a projection made at the start, not part of the freedom estimate.
  • Herd size: every farm has 100 animals, and the result changes with that number (the county).

These numbers were computed with the analytic (closed-form) build of this version.

Surveillance streams: which the model uses

In the model:

  • Owner reports: run all the time: an owner notices a visible wound at a close look, every 7 days, and the case becomes a confirmed detection after the reporting delay, which also covers the veterinarian's visit and the laboratory.
  • Inspection rounds: every 30 days, 23 of the 114 farms, 30 animals examined on each; an animal carrying larvae is found with the inspection sensitivity.

Not in the model:

  • Fly trapping: a positive fly trap counts as a confirmed detection, and the freedom estimate no longer applies once a trap is positive. Empty traps give no credit toward freedom, because traps can catch nothing in an area that has cases. A trap channel is not built in this version.
  • Wildlife surveillance (deer, feral swine, hunter reports): wildlife enters only as a source of introductions; the model has no wildlife surveillance stream, so wildlife reports add no evidence in the model, although they happen in practice.
  • Movement checks (pre-movement inspection and treatment at checkpoints and markets): not a surveillance stream. The share of infested moved animals that checks stop is an input the user sets, with no data behind it.
  • Slaughter inspection: not in the model's design.
  • Pets and human cases: not surveyed; outside the model's farms.

What the ranking does not cover: In the ranking for this version the starting state and the surveillance design are fixed in every draw, so the ranking says nothing about them. Herd size is drawn.

The earlier six-month scenario

The scenario of the page before this version is still in the app: 100 farms of 100 animals, 6 inspection rounds, one every 30 days, with 20 farms visited per round, 180 days, constant rates and the introduction module off. Its estimate at day 180 is 89 percent. The earlier ranking was computed on it, and the earlier two-build agreement check included a set of settings around it. Both are shown below the results for this version on their cards.

Rain, wind events and terrain are not in the model: see what the model leaves out.

What the model leaves out

  • Fly trapping: the model has no trap channel. The rule is: a positive fly trap counts as a confirmed detection, and the freedom estimate no longer applies once a trap is positive. Empty traps give no credit toward freedom, because traps can catch nothing in an area that has cases. A trap channel is not built in this version.
  • Season: in the county scenario introductions and spread between farms follow the monthly temperature of the county (season). Rain, wind events, terrain and local overwintering of pupae are left out, and so is the slowing of fly generations on a farm in winter. The six-month scenario holds the rates constant at their summer 2026 values.
  • Wildlife and pets: the model has no surveillance stream for them; they enter only through the introduction rate, so reports about them add no evidence in the model, although such reports do happen in practice. The model says nothing about freedom in wildlife.
  • Herds under 10 animals: outside the model's farms.
  • Pupae and the next fly generation: a farm stops seeding others when its animals stop carrying larvae; in the field, flies emerge about a week after the larvae drop and lay eggs about a week after that.
  • Controls after the last detection: quarantine, movement controls and sterile-fly releases are not states of the model. In the county scenario sterile-fly coverage, movement checks and preventive treatment are inputs the user sets, and they scale the rates (introductions).
  • Spread between farms inside a free zone: the model covers one zone. An infested farm can arise in two ways. Arrivals from outside the zone, including spread from infested areas nearby, enter through the introduction interval. Spread from farms inside the zone that are already infested is also in the model (the zone doubling time), but it acts only once a farm in the zone is infested. While the zone is free there is no infested farm inside it to spread from, so the only way it can stop being free is an introduction. For that reason spread between farms has almost no effect on the freedom estimate: in the model's design, changing the zone doubling time from 24 to 10 days moves the six-month probability of freedom by 0.0001. Spread inside a farm matters much more, because it sets how many animals on an infested farm carry larvae and show wounds, and those are what inspections and owners detect.
  • Introduction pathways: in the county scenario the introduction module splits the rate into flies arriving, moved animals and wildlife, with assumed shares. No data inform the shares, the wound factor or the effect of either mitigation. Nearby detections are a multiplier the user sets by hand. The lag of one fly generation between a sterile-fly release and its effect is left out. In the six-month scenario the introduction interval is one constant rate.
  • One county: the county scenario is a worked example. A statement about the whole state needs many counties and the spread between them, which this model does not have (the county).
  • Confirmation: a detection means a laboratory-confirmed case; false alarms are not modelled.

Field conditions for releasing a zone, and which of them the model covers: zone-release conditions and what the model covers.

Freedom in the model and in an APHIS declaration

In the model, the zone is free when none of its 100 farms is infested. This is not the APHIS release or freedom criterion. The APHIS response strategy (the Green Book, A-1.1, page 25 of the PDF) says:

A declaration of NWS freedom after an infestation in the United States would be based on surveillance for NWS that includes trapping of flies and visual inspection of animals for myiasis. Depending on specific weather and seasonal conditions in the area(s) of infestation, surveillance should be carried out for 3 months past the last NWS detection

and gives that as generally 3 to 4 fly life cycles during an outbreak. The model's probability is at most a supporting quantity beside that, not a substitute for it.

The model's equations

The core of the model in plain notation, written out from its design document. Rates are per day; a time on the page (days) becomes a rate as 1 / time, or ln 2 / time for a doubling time.

The zone: farms becoming infested and clearing

new infestations per day: b(K, t) = ((M − K) / M) × (λ + βeff(t) × K)
leaving the count: each farm at age τend, the first age at which N (πL(τ) + πI(τ)) < 1/2
after the first confirmed detection, also: d(K) = γrel × K
spread between farms: βeff(t) = l(t) × βmax × p̄shed(t)

Before any detection a farm leaves K only when its own infestation has run its course: 166 days after infestation at the central values. Each farm is fully counted until then, then gone; there is no variation between farms in when an infestation ends. Zone clearance, a steady exit whether or not the farm was found, is off in this scenario.

Mnumber of farms in the zone
K(t)number of infested farms at day t
λ = 1 / introduction intervalrate of new arrivals from outside, for the zone as a whole (it does not grow with M)
τendage at which a farm's own infestation has run its course (fewer than half an animal expected still infested); the farm leaves the count then, found or not (166 days at the central values)
γrel = 1 / release timeafter the first confirmed detection, rate at which each counted farm leaves (21 days on average, the zone clearance card's value, from the release rule for found and treated farms)
βmax = ln 2 / zone doubling timespread between farms with no control
l(t)the lockdown multiplier once a detection has been confirmed, otherwise 1
p̄shed(t)average share of animals carrying larvae, over the ages of the farms infested at day t

Rates that change over the run

in 30-day segment j of the run, λ is replaced by aj × λ and βeff(t) by mj × βeff(t)
introductions: aj = w (1 − pT eT) [ sF Aj S N + sM N (1 − eM) + sW Aj ]
spread between farms: mj = Aj S (1 − pT eT) (1 − φ eM)
sterile-fly factor: S = (1 + κ xref) / (1 + κ x)
fly activity: Aj = min(1, ½ [R(Tmax) + R(Tmin)] / R(27.2)), with R(T) = 0.00065 (T − 14.5) / (1 + 1.75T − 40) for T above 14.5 degrees C and 0 below

The multipliers are computed outside the two implementations by the introduction module (introductions and season). Under the reference conditions both are 1, and the model is the one above. The course inside a farm, both detection streams and the exits are not scheduled. The six-month scenario has both multipliers at 1 throughout.

sF, sM, sWshares of introductions from flies arriving, moved animals and wildlife (the remainder)
Ajfly activity in the month of segment j, from 0 to 1; Tmax and Tmin are the month's mean daily maximum and minimum temperature
x, xref, κshare of the sterile-fly release target being met, its reference (0.5), and the strength of the sterile-fly effect
Ndetections in nearby counties relative to summer 2026
wopen wounds on animals relative to usual
pT, eTshare of animals given preventive treatment, and how well it protects
eM, φshare of infested moved animals stopped by movement checks, and the share of spread between farms carried by moved animals

Inside one infested farm

dπL/dτ = βw πI πS − γL πL
dπI/dτ = γL πL − γR πI
dπR/dτ = γR πI, with πS = 1 − πL − πI − πR
share carrying larvae: pshed(τ) = πI(τ)
share with a visible wound: pclin(τ) = fmax (1 − e−τ/Tc) πI(τ)

Every infested farm runs this same course; there is no fly population and no pupal stage.

τdays since the farm was infested
πS, πL, πI, πRshares of the farm's animals: not infested, eggs laid but no larvae visible, carrying larvae, recovered (treated, healed or dead)
βw = ln 2 / within-premises doubling timespread between animals on the farm
γL = 1 / latent timeeggs laid to larvae visible
γR = 1 / within-premises recovery timean animal stops carrying larvae
fmax, Tcshare of wounds visible, and the clinical onset time

Detection

a visited farm passes inspection clean with chance E[(1 − Se)J], where X ~ Binomial(N, pshed(τ)) and J ~ Hypergeometric(N, X, n)
round r is all clean with chance Lr(K): the product of those chances over the infested farms among the visited ones
effective owner reporting rate: ρr,eff = 1 / (1 / ρr + Tlook / 2), which takes the place of ρr in the next line
owner reports from a farm of age τ, per day: h(τ) = ρr × [1 − (1 − ρa pclin(τ))N]

Detection means a confirmed case; false alarms are not modelled. The first detection sets the lockdown multiplier and the release clock on for the rest of the horizon.

N, nanimals on a farm, and animals examined per visited farm
Seinspection sensitivity: chance an inspector finds an examined animal that carries larvae
X, Janimals carrying larvae on the farm, and how many of them are among the n examined (drawn without replacement)
ρachance the owner notices a visible wound (per animal)
ρrowner reporting rate per day, about 1 / mean reporting delay
Tlookdays between the owner's close looks at the animals. A visible wound waits on average half of it for the next close look, so the mean delay from a visible wound to a report is 1 / ρr + Tlook / 2. A value of 0 leaves ρr unchanged.
Lr(K)chance inspection round r finds nothing when K farms are infested

The freedom calculation

Pfree(t) = P(K(t) = 0 | no confirmed detection through day t)

The chance of each value of K is carried forward in time. After each clean inspection round it is multiplied by Lr(K) and rescaled to sum to 1 (Bayes' rule); between rounds the same update runs continuously for "no owner report". At the start, K(0) is drawn from a Poisson distribution and each starting farm's age from an exponential distribution (see the county scenario).

Two implementations compute these same equations: an analytic calculation and a simulator of random histories (the agreement check).

DRAFT Draft model output under assumed rates; not evidence of freedom or absence.

Do two independent builds agree?

The agreement check for this version: PASS. The two builds agree on 41 evaluable cells at the last round, with 1 cell beyond 3 standard errors against an allowance of 1; five cells with very fast spread between farms disagree over rounds, and that gap was present before this version.

The fast-spread gap, diagnosed: a follow-up compared both builds with a third calculation that makes no approximation over ages. The simulator matches it. The analytic build is the one that is off. This is a limit of an approximation in that build (it gives every infested farm the same mix of ages), not a coding error. At the county scenario's setting, a zone doubling time of 24 days, the error in the chance the zone is free is at most about 0.0005 at any round. It grows as spread gets faster: under 0.002 at 3 days and up to about 0.02 at 0.25 days, where the analytic build reads too high from the second round on. The app shows a note below 3 days, and its slider stops at 0.25 days.

The 471-setting grid, rerun: an earlier rerun with new random draws did not pass the rule as written (5 settings beyond 3 standard errors, 2 allowed). Three of the five came from the two builds limiting a very short doubling time at different values. Both builds now use the same limits, and the grid was rerun with the simulator's original random draws and with new ones. Both runs pass the rule as written: 2 settings are beyond 3 standard errors in each, with 2 allowed. Taking the two runs together, 4 settings are beyond 3 standard errors against 2 allowed; three of the four did not repeat with 100,000 simulated histories. One real gap remains. At an extreme setting (the infestation doubles every 0.1 days on a farm and every day between farms, under very heavy inspection) the analytic build reads about 0.02 higher than the simulator, confirmed with 100,000 histories. The gap disappears when spread between farms is switched off, which points to the gap described in the paragraph above; the third calculation was not run at this setting. The earlier difference in limits had hidden it. Five settings that could never be compared, because nearly every simulated history raised an alarm, were replaced by a milder version of the same combination, and all five agree. The grid does not use the inputs new in this version; those are covered by the check above.

The check below is the earlier one, on the model before this version.

The interactive app runs the same analytic calculation as the numbers on this page.

Two implementations written independently from the same written design, an analytic (closed-form) calculation and a simulator (10,000 random histories per setting), were run on 471 comparisons: 94 parameter settings, nearly all read at five times from 30 to 180 days. The test grid is centred on a fixed set of test values, not on this page's six-month scenario. 53 could not be compared: 5 comparisons were lost to a simulator time-out, and 48 had nothing to compare against because no simulated history came through with clean surveillance data or the simulator's spread was zero.

Of the 418 that were compared, 1 gap was larger than three simulator standard deviations, against about 1.1 expected by chance (2 allowed). Reruns show this one is not chance: a small bias in the analytic calculation of about 0.004 at the extreme within-farm doubling time of 0.1 days, far below the parameter's range. The analytic calculation sat above the simulator in 196 comparisons and below it in 222 (sign test p = 0.22: no clear lean either way).

A separate check of 38 settings around the page's own six-month scenario found one gap: with no surveillance at all, an old leftover farm and spread between farms on, the analytic calculation reads about 0.008 low. No setting in that check with surveillance shows that gap; the checks bound the bias at the settings tested, not everywhere.

Agreement says the arithmetic matches the design. It does not say the design or the numbers are right.

The labels, defined once

Evidence (in the opening line of each parameter card), one of:

  • counted from reports: events counted in case reports for this setting
  • bounded by published sources: published sources set limits, and the value is chosen inside them
  • converted from a related setting: a rate observed for something else, converted by a formula
  • little data: a few observations or indirect figures, and the value is mostly judgement
  • no data: assumed: no source informs the value

What the value rests on (each card gives the one-line reason):

  • counted from reports events counted in case reports, news or compilations for this setting and turned into a rate by arithmetic
  • converted from a related setting a rate observed for something else (wild deer, a fly population) converted by a formula to this parameter
  • judgement within data chosen by judgement inside limits that observations set
  • guessed no source fixes it
  • operating setting a control setting the user chooses, informed by literature

No row is labelled "measured": no parameter is read directly off a study in a fitting setting.

Quotes found: how many of the quotes on the card's sources were found, word for word or as a near match, in the source text by machine. It shows the sources say what is quoted, not that the value is right.

Evidence mix: the kinds of sources on the card.

Census verdict (on each source line of the introduction interval, owner reporting delay, zone clearance time, within-premises recovery time, chance the owner notices a wound cards): the result of reading that source against what that card uses it for (below). A source on two cards has a verdict for each.

  • census: supports the source says what the card uses it for, in a setting the card states
  • census: partly supports part of the use holds; the card says which part does not
  • census: does not support the source does not say what it was cited for
  • census: could not open the page is behind a bot check or has been overwritten, with no archived copy

How to read the ranking

  • Range: everywhere on this page a parameter's range is its 90 percent interval: values were drawn so that 5 percent fall below the low end and 5 percent above the high end (a lognormal, Gamma or Beta curve fitted to the two ends). Most range ends are judgement; each card says which.
  • Variance share: the share of the spread in the six-month estimate across the draws that the parameter explains on its own, estimated from averages in 10 equal bins.
  • A wide range ranks high by construction: the ranking measures each range as set, and most ranges are judgement.
  • Conditional on the scenario: the starting state, the farm design and the surveillance design are fixed (see the six-month scenario), so the ranking says nothing about them; herds of 30 animals instead of 100 lower the six-month estimate from about 0.93 to about 0.88.

Introductions: where new infested farms come from

Everything that brings a new infested farm into the zone from outside is one rate. This module builds that rate from three sources and lets it change month by month.

The rate in words: the rate is the reference rate, one new infested farm about every 130 days, scaled by the three sources and their dials. Flies arriving follow fly activity, sterile-fly coverage and nearby detections. Moved animals follow nearby detections and movement checks. Wildlife follows fly activity. Open wounds and preventive treatment scale the total.

The calibration rule: under the reference conditions the result is exactly the reference rate. The reference conditions are a warm month, sterile-fly coverage at its reference, nearby detections as in summer 2026 and no added mitigation. The county scenario departs from them in one input: nearby detections are at 1.5.

What is assumed: the shares of the three sources, the wound factor and the effect of movement checks have no data behind them, and nearby detections are set by hand. Wildlife is a source of introductions only, not evidence.

How to read the introductions picture
  • The three orange boxes are the sources: "Flies arriving", "Moved animals" and "Wildlife", each with its share of introductions "in a warm month".
  • The blue dials under a source scale that source: "Season", "Sterile-fly coverage" and "Nearby detections" on flies arriving, "Movement checks" and "Nearby detections" on moved animals, and "Season" on wildlife.
  • "On the total": "Preventive treatment" and "Open wounds" scale the sum of the three.
  • "New infested farms per month" is the one arrow into "The zone". It is the "New arrivals from outside" input of the zone picture.
The equation, the symbols, the sterile-fly rule and spread between farms

The rate of new infested farms in month k is the reference rate times the wound factor, times the share of animals left unprotected by preventive treatment, times the sum of the three sources:

λk = λref × w × (1 − pT eT) × [ sF Ak S N + sM N (1 − eM) + sW Ak ]

λrefthe reference rate: introduction interval
sF, sM, sWshare of introductions from flies arriving and share of introductions from moved animals; wildlife is the remainder (0.6, 0.25 and 0.15)
Akfly activity in month k, from 0 to 1 (season)
Sthe sterile-fly factor, from share of the sterile-fly release target being met and strength of the sterile-fly effect
Ndetections in nearby counties, relative to summer 2026
wopen wounds on animals, relative to usual
pT, eTshare of animals given preventive treatment and how well preventive treatment protects an animal
eMshare of infested moved animals stopped by movement checks

Under the reference conditions the bracket is 1. At the values of the county scenario, where nearby detections are at 1.5, the bracket is 1.425 in a warm month and 0.574 in January.

The sterile-fly rule: with the share x of the release target met, the fertile share of matings is 1 / (1 + κ x). This is the ratio rule of Knipling, as reported by Krafsur (1994), with the competitiveness of sterile males folded into κ. The module uses the fertile share relative to the reference coverage of 0.5, so S = (1 + κ × 0.5) / (1 + κ x). No release records are used. The lag of one fly generation between a release and its effect is left out.

Nearby detections: a multiplier the user sets by hand. A value of 1 is the level of summer 2026. The county scenario uses 1.5, from a count of recent cases near the county (the basis and its limits). No formula from counts by distance and direction is built.

Spread between farms is carried by flies and by moved animals, so it has its own multiplier: mk = Ak S (1 − pT eT) (1 − φ eM), where φ is the share of spread between farms carried by moved animals. The cut after a detection still applies on top (the zone).

The twelve parameters for introductions and season
  • Share of introductions from flies arriving: the "Flies arriving" source on the introductions picture
  • Share of introductions from moved animals: the "Moved animals" source on the introductions picture
  • Share of the sterile-fly release target being met: the "Sterile-fly coverage" dial on "Flies arriving" on the introductions picture
  • Strength of the sterile-fly effect: not drawn; it sets how strongly the "Sterile-fly coverage" dial acts on the introductions picture
  • Detections in nearby counties, relative to summer 2026: the two "Nearby detections" dials, on "Flies arriving" and on "Moved animals", on the introductions picture
  • Open wounds on animals, relative to usual: the "Open wounds" dial on the total on the introductions picture
  • Share of animals given preventive treatment: the "Preventive treatment" dial on the total on the introductions picture
  • How well preventive treatment protects an animal: not drawn; it sets how strongly the "Preventive treatment" dial acts on the introductions picture
  • Share of infested moved animals stopped by movement checks: the "Movement checks" dial on "Moved animals" on the introductions picture
  • Share of spread between farms carried by moved animals: not drawn; it acts on "Spread between farms" on the zone picture
  • Warmer or cooler than normal: the "Daily high" and "Daily low" rows on the season picture, which it shifts together
  • Month of the last detection: the dashed line "The clock starts in June" on the season picture

The detailed formulas, with every symbol defined: the model's equations.

Season: fly activity by month

The fly is less active in the cold. Fly activity in a month runs from 0 to 1 and is set by the monthly temperature of the county. It scales the flies arriving, the wildlife source and spread between farms.

How to read the result

A cold month has fewer introductions, so the chance that the zone is free rises in winter and falls back when the weather warms. That rise is lower pressure, not stronger evidence. Read the warm-season value. On the county scenario the model estimate (draft) is 85 percent in July, rises to 94 percent in January and is 85 percent at the last round in May.

Daily high and low: the mean daily maximum and minimum temperature of the month in degrees C (Crystal City (USC00412160), 1991 to 2020 normals, inside the county). Activity: fly activity, from 0 to 1. Introductions: the rate of new infested farms as a percent of the reference rate, at the values of the county scenario. It is above 100 in the warm months because nearby detections are set at 1.5 times the summer 2026 level. Fly activity is below one half in January, February, March, November and December.

How to read the season picture
  • The orange bars are "Fly activity, 0 to 1 (1 = a warm month)", one bar for each month, with its value above it.
  • "Daily high, C" and "Daily low, C" are the mean daily maximum and minimum temperature of the month, the two numbers the activity is computed from.
  • The blue shading marks a cold month: the colder the month, the darker the band.
  • The dashed line is "The clock starts in June (the last detection)". A run passes through the months from there.
The activity curve, and what is assumed

Fly activity comes from the development-rate curve of Gutierrez and Ponti (2014, equation 1):

R(T) = 0.00065 (T − 14.5) / (1 + 1.75T − 40) per hour for T above 14.5 degrees C, and 0 below
Ak = min(1, ½ [R(Tmax) + R(Tmin)] / R(27.2))

  • Assumed, not sourced: that fly activity scales with the development rate; the reference temperature of 27.2 degrees C, which is the source's survival optimum; and averaging over the daily high and low, which keeps some activity in months whose mean sits near the threshold.
  • The cap at 1 follows the source: hot months are not limiting in Texas.
  • Inside a farm the season does not act: eggs and larvae are on the host at body temperature.
  • Not modelled: rain, wind events, terrain and local overwintering of pupae.
  • Steps: the run moves in steps of 30 days, not calendar months.

Inputs: warmer or cooler than normal and month of the last detection. The formula with every symbol is in the model's equations.

The county: Zavala County, Texas

One county is a worked example. A statement about the whole state needs many counties and the spread between them, which this model does not have.

Why this county: Zavala County is the index county of the 2026 outbreak in Texas. Its three confirmed cases, on 3, 5 and 11 June 2026, form a short timeline. Its census figures are complete, and a weather station with temperature normals sits inside it.

Farms and herd sizes: the zone is the county's 114 operations with cattle (2022 Census of Agriculture), each taken as one farm of 100 animals. The real herds differ widely: the mean is 335 head and the median size class is 20 to 49 head. At the last round the result is 0.77 at 35 animals, 0.85 at 100 animals and 0.91 at 335 animals, so the single herd size is a limitation.

The run and its results: the fixed inputs of the run on this county, the surveillance streams and the headline results are on the county scenario.

The detection timeline, the herd sizes and the limits of the data

The detection timeline

  • Confirmed cases: three, on 3, 5 and 11 June 2026 (the official record of confirmed detections, pulled on 17 November 2026).
  • Zone released: 3 September 2026, 84 days after the last confirmation.
  • Since then: the county was named in a new zone order dated 13 November 2026, with no new case in the county in the official record.
  • The clock starts in June, at the last detection.

Herd sizes in the census

38,198 cattle on 114 operations. The mean is far above the median size class because 12 operations with 500 or more head hold 30,556 of the cattle. The model uses one herd size for every farm, and 100 lies between the two.

Limits of the county data

  • An operation in the census is not the same as a premises. Wildlife, feral swine and pets are outside these counts.
  • The census figures have no second-source check.
  • The temperature normals of the station rest on fewer than the full 30 years of record.
  • The dates are confirmation dates, and the zone dates were read from the state agency's list of orders, not from the orders.

Sources and pull dates: what changed in this version. Where the introductions come from: introductions. The months of the run: season.

Zone-release conditions and what the model covers

Field staff weigh a list of conditions when they consider releasing a zone. The model speaks to some of them and not to others. The table marks each condition as covered, partly covered or left out, and says what is to be confirmed by hand. In this version 0 of the 7 conditions are covered, 4 are partly covered and 3 are left out.

Over every county in the record it is 5.6, and most of those cases are far to the west, in New Mexico, Arizona and far west Texas. The choice of 400 km is judgement. Introduction interval

Value: one new infested farm arrives in the zone about every 130 days. Evidence: counted from reports. Assumed: An active quarantine zone lies next to the zone for the whole period, and a rate counted per county applies to the zone unchanged.

The model assumes 130 days; the range explored is 50 to 400 days.

What this is: The average number of days between new infestations arriving in the zone from outside it (flies flying in, moved animals or wildlife), one rate for the whole zone. In the zone picture it is the "New arrivals from outside" input. It counts arrivals from outside the zone. As fitted, it also carries spread from infested areas next to the zone (see how the value was reached); the zone's own spread term is separate and has almost no effect on freedom.

Detail and sources

Checked against the official record in this version: the first cases behind this count were taken from a public online encyclopedia's case table. The official record of confirmed detections, pulled on 17 November 2026, lists the same counties with the same totals through 31 August 2026. The nine counted introductions keep their dates, except the Starr County case, which moves by one day. The value is not recounted in this version, and the cases confirmed since 31 August are not in it (what changed in this version).

Value: 130 d, range 50 to 400 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.117.

What the value rests on: counted from reports The first cases were counted from news reports and a public case compilation, then divided by a time window and by a judged number of at-risk counties. The value fails the page's rule for a high-impact parameter.

Quote check on this card's sources: 4 quotes: 4 found word for word. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value of 130 days (range 50 to 400) applies to a free county next to an active zone. The AI literature review dated the first case in every Texas county in summer 2026 [C-2.1, C-2.2, C-2.7a, C-2.7b]. Six far-apart counties seeded within ten days of the first case, and one later far jump (Jim Hogg, 25 June), were set aside as spread that took place before anyone knew of the outbreak. Nine later first cases (20 June to 16 August) all bordered an active quarantine zone and were counted as introductions, so spread from infested areas next door is part of this rate. Nine events over the AI literature review's 85-day window, spread across 12 to 20 at-risk counties, give 0.005 to 0.009 introductions per county per day, which is a mean interval of 110 to 190 days, and 130 days was picked inside that span. The nine dates span 57 days (20 June to 16 August), and the review does not say what period the 85 days covers. Over 57 days the same arithmetic gives 76 to 127 days, which is below the chosen 130. If the rule is read literally, as a county sharing a border with a county that already had a case, Medina County would be dropped. None of its neighbours had a confirmed case by its first case on 24 June (Uvalde's first case came on 29 June), although Uvalde had been in a quarantine zone since 3 June [C-2.2]. That reading leaves eight events, or 0.0047 to 0.0078 per county per day over the 85 days, which is an interval of 128 to 213 days with the chosen 130 at the lower edge, according to the source census. The Medina date appears in the case compilation [C-2.1] and in a dated case list relaying the USDA dashboard [C-2.2], and the other news article cited with it gives no Medina date [C-2.7b]. The figure of 12 to 20 at-risk counties is the AI literature review's judgement, and no source gives the ring of at-risk counties. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly. A first case is dated by laboratory confirmation rather than by arrival, and a county is not necessarily the model's zone, where a larger zone means a shorter interval. The range ends are judgement. A model paper's seeding rate [C-2.6] was used only as a consistency check. This is the top parameter, accounting for about half the variance in six-month freedom, and it fails the page's own rule for high-impact parameters (step 4 of the review process), because its evidence is a public compilation and news reports, with no primary source and no expert elicitation. Official case records with dates would remedy that. Every case date behind the count comes from a public online encyclopedia's case table [C-2.1] and a syndicated news article [C-2.2], and no quote from these sources carries those dates. The 4 quotes found on this card's sources give context (long-distance spread [C-2.4] and a model's seeding rate [C-2.6]) rather than the dates that were counted.

What the sources do not tell us

No official linkage of any 2026 case is in the sources reviewed, so the sources do not say which introductions were moved animals and which were flies, or whether the at-risk ring really held 12 to 20 counties.

Owner reporting delay

Value: 3 days on average from the owner noticing a wound to a confirmed detection. Evidence: little data. Assumed: The value and the upper end of the range are judgement above a floor set by three timed cases.

There is little good data for this value. The model assumes 3 days; the range explored is 1 to 12.5 days.

Detail and sources

What this is: How fast a wound the owner has noticed becomes a confirmed detection, set as a daily rate; one over the rate is the mean delay in days. In the model pictures it is part of "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture and the "Owner reports" input on the zone picture. It starts when the owner notices (the time for a wound to become visible and to be noticed is not in it) and it ends at confirmation, not at the owner's call: the model treats a detection as a confirmed one and has no separate laboratory step, so the time from the call to laboratory confirmation sits inside this delay.

What the delay covers

The domain experts break the time from a fly laying eggs to a confirmed case into four parts. The model lumps the last three into this one delay, so it covers more than the owner's wait:

  1. Fly to noticing: from egg laying until the owner sees a wound. Not in this delay: the latent time and the chance a sick animal is noticed cover it.
  2. Owner waits: the owner has seen something but looks closely days later. In this delay.
  3. Veterinary sampling: a veterinarian or official comes out to sample and ships it. In this delay.
  4. Laboratory: from receipt to confirmation, "several days" (domain experts; no written source). One 2026 preprint reports 3 to 7 day testing bottlenecks (Garcia, abstract only, a background claim, not a measurement). In this delay.

The parts are not built up into the 3 days.

Outside the range: the naive-area figure on this card (Florida 2016, a mean of about 14 days) lies above the range's 12.5-day end, and the APHIS response strategy (A-1.1, page 18 of the PDF) records that in the 2016 to 2017 Florida outbreak samples were not sent to NVSL for identification until 84 days after presumptive positive identification by local veterinarians. The range does not cover it.

Value: 0.33 /d (mean 3 d), range 0.08 to 1.0 /d (mean delay 1 to 12.5 d) (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.089.

What the value rests on: judgement within data Three timed cases set a floor of about 1.5 to 2 days. The 3 days and the 12.5-day upper end are judgement.

Quote check on this card's sources: 7 quotes: 6 found word for word, 1 near match. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is a mean delay of 3 days (a rate of 0.33 per day), with a range of 1 to 12.5 days (rates of 1.0 to 0.08 per day). Three timed cases were found. In the first, the manager of a ranch in Zavala County found a calf's wound on a routine check, and the laboratory confirmed it 2.5 days later [B-3.7]. This is the only case timed from the owner. In the second, a household dog from Lea County, New Mexico, was seen at a veterinary clinic in Andrews County, Texas, on Saturday 6 June 2026 [B-3.19]. The news report gives confirmation on Monday 8 June, but a case table based on APHIS data dates it 7 June [C-2.1], so the interval is 1 to 2 days. Its clock starts at the clinic, so the owner's own delay is missing, and because the dog's travel history is unknown, the case is perhaps better read as evidence of an introduction. In the third, at Sabinas Hidalgo, Mexico, a heifer recently moved to a certified feedlot was detected officially on 20 September 2025 and confirmed on 21 September, an interval of 1 day [B-3.10, B-3.9]. It was not an owner report, so it times only the sampling and laboratory steps. Texas rules ask for a report within 24 hours of a suspect case [B-3.8], but this states what owners are required to do and is not a measured delay. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly. Two of the three intervals leave out the owner's step and therefore understate the delay, so their average of about 1.5 to 2 days is a floor rather than an estimate. All three cases come from areas on alert during an active response, whereas the six-month scenario applies the same 3 days after release, when alertness may have fallen. The AI literature review's alternative for a naive area, from Florida 2016, is a rate of 0.07 per day (a mean of about 14 days), and it is not used in the headline estimate. The 3 days and the 12.5-day upper end are the AI literature review's judgement.

What the sources do not tell us

No per-case dates of noticing, reporting and confirmation are in the sources reviewed, so the sources do not say how long owners actually wait between first noticing a wound and calling it in.

Zone clearance time

Value: 21 days on average from a new detection to the release of each farm still counted, and not used before a detection. Evidence: bounded by published sources. Assumed: The agency release rule for found and treated farms sets the clock for every counted farm.

The model assumes 21 days; the range explored is 7 to 40 days.

Detail and sources

What this is: The average number of days before a counted farm is removed from the zone's infested count by clearance. It plays no part in any freedom number: clearance is off for farms nobody has found, which leave the count only when their own infestation has run its course (see the equations card). The 21 days is used only after a new confirmed detection, as the release clock: from then on each counted farm leaves at that rate, standing for the release rule for found and treated farms. The model pictures do not draw the release clock; the clock starts at a confirmed detection, a farm drawn as "Found" on the zone picture.

Value: 21 d, after a new detection only (off before), range 7 to 40 d (90 percent interval); no effect on six-month freedom (not drawn in the ranking).

What the value rests on: judgement within data The value rests on an agency release rule and on news snapshots of active cases, which time paperwork rather than biology, and the tails are judgement. It is used only after a new detection, so it does not move freedom.

Quote check on this card's sources: 8 quotes: 7 found word for word, 1 near match. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 21 days, with a range of 7 to 40. It sets only the release clock after a new detection, so it does not move freedom. It rests on two kinds of evidence. The first is the release rule. A treated animal is re-inspected 24 hours after treatment and released once no live larvae remain and an official veterinarian signs off [C-3.1], and the Green Book keeps animals in quarantine until the wounds heal [C-3.2]. The second is how long Texas 2026 cases stayed on the active list, read from news snapshots of active counts on 30 June, 6 August, 18 August and 3 September [C-2.2, B-2.22, B-2.17, A-3.18]. Each case is only bracketed between two dates (for example 25 to 62 days, or 0 to 19 days) and is not timed. A fit that treats each of 46 Texas cases as such a bracket (interval-censored maximum likelihood) gives a mean of 18.7 days with an exponential curve and 20.1 days with a lognormal curve (median 14.8 days), and the spread is wide. The count of four active cases on 3 September is the AI literature review's reading, because that tracker page has since been overwritten. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly, because it times the administrative clock rather than the biology. The first Texas calf's wound healed in a week [B-3.7], and its case was off the active list by 30 June [C-2.2], at most 27 days after its confirmation on 3 June, but no source says how much sooner it left the list. The times are also per animal case and interval-censored, not per premises. A 21-day Texas release rule seen only in a search summary could not be verified. The tails (7 and 40 days) are judgement, and the AI literature review rated them as low confidence.

What the sources do not tell us

The release rule and the case lists time paperwork rather than fly output, so the sources do not say when a cleared premises actually stops producing flies, which is what matters for spread.

Within-premises recovery time

Value: 7 days on average for an infested animal to stop carrying larvae. Evidence: bounded by published sources. Assumed: The value is a mix of treated and untreated animals, and the share treated early is not known.

The model assumes 7 days; the range explored is 3 to 15 days.

What this is: The average number of days one animal carries live larvae, until treatment, the larvae leaving, or death ends it. In the farm picture it is the Infested to Recovered step. It moves animals, and it also sets when a farm nobody has found leaves the zone's infested count: at the end of its infestation's course, 166 days after infestation at the central values, or about 9 days at a 3-day recovery, when the infestation dies out on its own.

Detail and sources

Value: 7 d, range 3 to 15 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.015.

What the value rests on: judgement within data The sources bound the treated and untreated courses, and the 7-day mix of the two is a modelling choice.

Quote check on this card's sources: 12 quotes: 10 found word for word, 2 near matches. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 7 days, with a range of 3 to 15. Larvae feed for 5 to 7 days after hatching and then leave the wound [A-3.1, A-3.2, A-3.4]. Untreated wounds attract more egg-laying, and the animal dies in 5 to 10 days [A-3.4], 7 to 10 days [A-3.7], 7 to 14 days [A-3.8], or one to two weeks [A-3.1]. The AI literature review put the untreated larvae-bearing period at 6 to 12 days, with a central value of 10. In a trial, doramectin given 2 hours before first-stage larvae were placed in wounds cleared them within 24 to 48 hours [A-3.13]. That trial tested preventive dosing against young larvae rather than treatment of an established wound, so it bounds the treated course only loosely, and the federal procedure's re-inspection 24 hours after treatment [C-3.1] is closer. On that reading, an animal found on day 3 to 5 and treated carries larvae for 3 to 6 days. The 7 days is a mix of treated and untreated animals under surveillance, and the mix is a modelling choice rather than data. Figures that time something else were set aside as too long. These are the 15 to 17 days of a Mexican model's "infection process" [A-3.12] and the roughly 22 days of Mexico's active-case list [A-3.17], both of which run to wound healing. The model paper gives no end point for its infection process, and reading it as running to wound healing is the AI literature review's interpretation. A different value applies in one case. If the model already removes reported animals by treatment, the AI literature review recommends 10 days (6 to 17) for the undetected course instead.

What the sources do not tell us

The files do not give the real share of infested animals that are treated early rather than left alone, which sets the 7-day mix.

Chance the owner notices a wound

Value: 0.70, the chance for each animal with a visible wound that the owner notices it. Evidence: no data: assumed. Assumed: An alert owner notices most visible wounds.

There is no data for this value. The model assumes 0.70; the range explored is 0.45 to 0.90.

Detail and sources

What this is: The chance that an owner notices a visible screwworm wound on an infested animal. In the model pictures it is part of "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture and the "Owner reports" input on the zone picture. It applies only to wounds that have already become visible (the visible-wound ramp comes before it); the time from noticing to confirmation is the separate reporting delay. In the model this chance applies to each animal on the farm that has a visible wound. The more animals have visible wounds, the more likely it is that the owner has noticed at least one of them, and the farm reports at the reporting rate multiplied by that likelihood (the equation is shown below). The chance is therefore not a single decision, made once, about whether a wound will ever be noticed. While its wounds stay visible, the farm can still be reported on any later day.

Where it enters the model: The owner-report rate of a farm infested τ days ago is h(τ) = ρr × [1 − (1 − ρa pclin(τ))N], where ρa is this chance, ρr is the reporting rate, pclin(τ) is the share of animals with a visible wound, and N is the number of animals on the farm. It is the last equation in the detection part of the model's equations.

Value: 0.70, range 0.45 to 0.90 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.028.

What the value rests on: guessed No study measures this chance, and no source on this card informs it directly. The value is a judgement made with indirect numbers in view.

Quote check on this card's sources: 7 quotes: 6 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

No source on this card measures or directly informs this chance, so the chosen value of 0.70 and its range of 0.45 to 0.90 are a judgement. The sources describe related quantities, which are set out below together with the reason each one does not give the chance the model needs. Mexico handled 10,511 animal myiasis reports from 1 January 2024 to 1 November 2025, and larvae from 9,049 of them were identified as screwworm [B-2.7]. Set against the 9,574 cases that the same bulletin confirms to the same end date (counted from 21 November 2024, when the outbreak's case count starts), the ratio is about 95 percent. This ratio compares identifications from reports with confirmed cases. It is not the share of cases found through reports, because one case can give several reports and the two counts start on different dates. It shows that most cases are found through owners and veterinarians, but it cannot say how many infested animals nobody reported, because those animals appear in neither count. In Florida in 2016, 3 of 9 pet cases (33 percent) surfaced only through a later questionnaire [B-2.1]. These were animals that veterinarians had seen, so the figure measures missed reporting in a naive area rather than owners failing to notice a wound. For wild Key deer, biologists estimated one undetected death for each known one [B-2.2], which describes the finding of carcasses in wildlife rather than a handled herd. Handling frequency comes from a 2015 online forum thread of small cattle producers, with answers ranging from daily to weekly [B-2.18], and from a recommendation to check animals daily [B-2.19]. The AI literature review's tally of 17 US posters in that thread does not reproduce, because the saved page has about 15 answers that give a frequency, two of them from Canada. None of these numbers is the per-animal chance the model needs. The central value and both range ends are judgement, and the recorded verdict is guessed.

What the sources do not tell us

No study in the sources reviewed measures what fraction of infested animals in an alert commercial herd go unnoticed.

Within-premises doubling time

Value: 3.6 days for the number of infested animals on a farm to double, before any recover. Evidence: converted from a related setting. Assumed: Growth rates of wild deer deaths and of fly populations apply to spread between animals on one farm.

The model assumes 3.6 days; the range explored is 3.2 to 3.9 days.

What this is: How fast infestation spreads between animals on one farm, set as a doubling time before any animals recover. In the farm picture it is the Susceptible to Latent step, driven by the "their flies lay eggs on more animals" loop from Infested. It stands in for the local flies; the model has no fly population and no pupal stage.

Detail and sources

What it implies (derived, not an input): this value is a gross rate, before animals recover. With latent time 2 days and recovery 7 days at their central values, the net doubling time of a farm's infestation is about 19 days, and each infested animal leads to 1.35 more (the outbreak on a farm grows only above 1). Across this card's range (3.2 to 3.9 days) that number runs from 1.24 to 1.52, above 1 across the whole range (net doubling about 13 to 27 days). The derivation above leaves out the 2-day latent stage, which slows early growth, so this net figure is longer than the net doubling the value was derived from.

Value: 3.6 d, range 3.2 to 3.9 d (at the central recovery time) (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.014.

What the value rests on: converted from a related setting The value is converted by a formula from the growth rates of wild deer deaths and of fly populations, and it is applied to spread between animals on one farm. There is no direct measurement.

Quote check on this card's sources: 10 quotes: 10 found word for word. See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 3.6 days, with a range of 3.2 to 3.9. It is derived rather than observed. Observed doublings of case counts are net of recovery. The uncontrolled Key deer deaths (4, 7, 20 and 96 per month, July to October 2016) double every 13 to 20 days [A-5.8]. A five-fold rise per fly generation, which was Knipling's design assumption [A-5.2], over a generation of about 21 days [A-5.4] doubles every 9 days. A fly-population model gives a potential doubling time of 14 days [A-5.1]. The model's parameter is the gross rate, so the recovery rate was added back with the formula gross doubling = 1 / (1/net doubling + 1/(0.69 x recovery time)). With a recovery time of 7 to 14 days, this gives 3.2 to 7.7 days across the AI literature review's table, with a central value of 4.5. The model's own within-premises recovery time is 7 days, not about 14, so the value is derived at 7 days. Net doublings of 9, 13.4 and 20 days give 3.15, 3.56 and 3.90 days, hence the central value of 3.6 and the range of 3.2 to 3.9. The value is tied to the recovery time. Across recovery times of 3 to 15 days the consistent value runs from 1.7 to 6.8 days, and in the ranking it is derived in each draw from a sampled net doubling (9 to 20 days) and that draw's recovery time. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly. The deer series counts deaths of wild deer across whole islands, and the other two sources describe fly-population growth, not animals on one premises. The same report and series is also the main input to the zone doubling time [C-1.4], which describes spread between farms. The formula is the AI literature review's, and because the model's instant recruitment ignores the 18 to 24 day fly generation, early growth runs fast. The Texas 2026 outbreak (47 cases on 38 premises) [A-5.13a] was used as a consistency check only.

What the sources do not tell us

No direct measurement of spread between animals on one premises is in the sources reviewed.

Share of wounds visible

Value: 0.9, the share of infested animals whose wound ever becomes visible. Evidence: little data. Assumed: Few infestations stay hidden, as estimated from tallies of cases that were found.

There is little good data for this value. The model assumes 0.9; the range explored is 0.75 to 0.98.

Detail and sources

What this is: The share of infested animals whose wound eventually becomes visible to someone looking carefully; the rest sit in hidden places such as nostrils, genitals or deep pockets. The model pictures do not draw visible wounds; this share acts through "Owner reports a wound" on the farm picture, on animals at the Infested step. It acts on owner reporting only; inspection uses its own chance, the inspection sensitivity.

Value: 0.9, range 0.75 to 0.98 (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom +0.014.

What the value rests on: judgement within data No study counts hidden infestations, and the value is an estimate from site tallies of cases that were found.

Quote check on this card's sources: 6 quotes: 5 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 0.9, with a range of 0.75 to 0.98. No study counts how many infestations stay hidden on a careful look. Reference texts all name the same hard sites, namely the nostrils, anus, prepuce, vagina and deep pocket wounds, where slight movement may be the only sign [A-4.1, A-4.2, A-4.3]. A Colombian cattle study lists barbed-wire injuries in 32.7 percent of 49 cases and the navel and scrotum in 18.4 percent each [A-4.4], and the AI literature review read this as 70 percent or more of cases at plainly visible sites. Newborns are an estimated 80 percent of potential livestock cases, mostly at the navel [A-4.7]. The evidence does not match the parameter exactly. A site tally includes only cases that someone found, so hidden cases are missing from it and the visible share is pushed up. The Colombian quote was also not found verbatim, and because wire injury is a cause while the navel and scrotum are sites, the sum may double count. The 0.9 and its range are an educated estimate, as the AI literature review itself calls them. The hidden share here (10 percent at the central value) and the 15 to 25 percent at hidden sites assumed on the inspection sensitivity card are two separate judgements, and they do not agree.

What the sources do not tell us

No study in the sources reviewed counts how many infestations stay hidden on a careful look at a US herd.

Mean latent time

Value: 2 days on average from eggs laid in a wound to larvae present. Evidence: bounded by published sources. Assumed: The same latent time holds at Texas temperatures.

The model assumes 2 days; the range explored is 1 to 3 days.

What this is: The average number of days from eggs laid in a wound to larvae present and visible. In the farm picture it is the Latent to Infested step. An animal still in the eggs-laid state cannot be found by inspection and does not pass infestation on.

Detail and sources

Value: 2 d, range 1 to 3 d (90 percent interval); average effect on six-month freedom -0.019.

What the value rests on: judgement within data Life-history summaries agree on 1 to 3 days. The two trials time the interval from wounding to detection, so they bound the value only loosely.

Quote check on this card's sources: 7 quotes: 6 found word for word, 1 not found (not shown). See where it enters the model

How the value was reached

The chosen value is 2 days, with a range of 1 to 3. Eggs hatch in 10 to 12 hours [A-1.1], 12 to 24 hours [A-1.2, A-1.3] or 10 to 21 hours [A-1.4]. Larvae are hard to see for the first day or two [A-1.3] and are visible by the third day [A-1.1], and disease can show as early as 1 to 2 days after egg laying [A-1.2]. Two field trials with regular inspection found infestations by day 3 to 5 after wounding in Mexico [A-1.7] and in 9 of 10 untreated castration wounds by the day-3 check in Argentina [A-1.8]. The early detections in Mexico were in the ivermectin group, where the drug failed, and the untreated controls were infested by day 8, as on the clinical onset card. There is a minor mismatch between the evidence and the parameter. The trials count from the day of wounding rather than the day the eggs were laid, so day 3 to 5 is an upper bound on latency plus the time to notice. The Mexican authors also found larvae older than expected, which suggests that young larvae were being missed. The life-history sources agree on 1 to 3 days, and the trials are consistent with that span without timing it, so the value of 2 days (1 to 3) is supported. The range ends match the span of the life-history sources. The Argentine quote was not found verbatim in the source.

What the sources do not tell us

Temperature is noted to move hatching by hours, but no Texas measurement is in the sources reviewed, so the sources do not say how latency shifts with Texas temperatures.
